t.4.65.1: Seeing the monkey host, many hundreds of thousands strong, thus dejected, Jāmbavān then spoke to Hanumān.
t.4.65.3: O Hanumān, you are truly the equal of Sugrīva, king of the monkeys, and of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa as well, in splendor and in strength.
t.4.65.2: Then he spoke the whole of his counsel: “O hero of the world of monkeys, Hanumān, why do you keep silent, having withdrawn to a solitary place, and say nothing?”
t.4.65.5: Many times indeed have I seen that mighty bird in the ocean, of great speed and great fame, snatching up serpents.
t.4.65.4: The two sons of Ariṣṭanemi: Vainateya of great strength, renowned like Garutmān, the foremost of all birds.
t.4.65.6: Whatever strength lies in his two wings, just so much is the strength of your arms; your prowess and your speed, too, fall in no way short of that.
t.4.65.7: O best of monkeys, your strength, intelligence, energy and courage are pre-eminent among all beings; why do you not know yourself?
t.4.65.8: Puñjikasthalā, a renowned apsaras and the foremost among the apsarases, became widely known as Añjanā, the wife of the monkey Kesarin.
t.4.65.9: Because of a curse, dear one, she became a she-monkey able to take any form at will, the daughter of the great-souled lord of monkeys, Kuñjara.
t.4.65.10: Though a monkey by birth, she was lovely in every limb and could take any form she wished; once, assuming a human body, she shone with the finest bloom of youth.
t.4.65.11: Adorned with colorful garlands and ornaments and clad in costly silk, she wandered on the summit of the mountain, which resembled a rain cloud of the monsoon season.
t.4.65.12: As that large-eyed woman stood upon the summit of the mountain, the wind gently carried away her beautiful yellow garment with its red border.
t.4.65.13: Then he saw her rounded, close-set thighs, her full breasts pressed together, and her well-formed, lovely face.
t.4.65.14: The moment he saw her, the illustrious one with broad, full hips, a slender waist and every limb lovely, Pavana was bewildered by desire.
t.4.65.15: Māruta, every limb of his body possessed by Manmatha and his mind carried away, embraced that blameless woman with his two stout arms.
t.4.65.16: But she, a woman of virtuous conduct, alarmed right there, spoke these words: "Who wishes to destroy this vow of fidelity to one husband?"
t.4.65.17: Having heard the words of Añjanā, Māruta replied: "I do not harm you, O lady of fair hips; let there be no fear for you, O fortunate one."
t.4.65.18: Because I have embraced you and come to you only in mind, O glorious lady, a son will be born to you who is valiant and endowed with intelligence.
t.4.65.19: Then, as a child in the great forest, seeing the risen sun and thinking it a fruit, you, eager to seize it, leapt up and flew into the sky.
t.4.65.20: Having then travelled three hundred yojanas, O great monkey, though buffeted by his blazing energy, I did not give way to despair.
t.4.65.21: Then, O great monkey, as you were swiftly rushing up into the sky, the wise Indra, filled with anger, hurled his thunderbolt at you.
t.4.65.22: Then, upon the topmost peak of the mountain, your left jaw was broken; and it is from this that your name is proclaimed as Hanumān.
t.4.65.23: Then, seeing you struck down, Vāyu himself, the bearer of fragrance, the shatterer, greatly enraged, did not blow at all in the three worlds.
t.4.65.24: When the three worlds were thrown into turmoil, all the gods, the lords of the worlds, were alarmed, and they sought to appease the enraged Māruta.
t.4.65.25: And when Pavana had been appeased, Brahmā granted you a boon, dear one of true valor: that in battle you could not be slain by any weapon.
t.4.65.26: And seeing you unharmed even by the stroke of the thunderbolt, the thousand-eyed one, pleased at heart, granted you a supreme boon.
t.4.65.27: "And may your death come only by your own free will, O lord," so it was said. You are thus the son of Kesarin, born of his wife, of terrible valour.
t.4.65.28: You are the true-born son of Māruta, and in splendour too you are his equal. For you, dear child, are the son of Vāyu, and in leaping as well you are his equal.
t.4.65.29: Today we are as good as lifeless; now, among us, you alone, endowed with skill and valour, are like a second king of birds.
t.4.65.31: At that time, by command of the gods, we gathered the herbs by which the amṛta was produced; then our strength was great.
t.4.65.30: Dear son, at the time of Trivikrama's strides I circled the earth, with its mountains, woods and forests, three times seven times, keeping it always to my right.
t.4.65.32: I, that same one, am now old and my prowess has declined; at this present time it is you, sir, endowed with every virtue, who must act for us.
t.4.65.33: Therefore, valiant one, rouse yourself and expand, for you are the best of those who leap; this entire army of monkeys longs to behold your prowess.
t.4.65.35: All the monkeys are despondent; O Hanumān, why do you stand by unconcerned? Stride forth, you of mighty speed, as Viṣṇu strode his three strides.
t.4.65.34: Rise, O tiger among monkeys, and leap across the great ocean, for, O Hanumān, the course that is yours surpasses that of all beings.
t.4.65.36: Then, urged on by Jāmbavant, the monkey, son of the Wind, renowned for his speed, gladdening that army of monkey heroes, assumed at that moment a mighty form.
